Family Health

Vaginal microbes: symptoms, infections and probiotic limits

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The vagina naturally contains a community of microorganisms, often called its microbiome or flora. A change in discharge, odour, itching or urinary comfort can have several explanations. “An imbalance” is not a complete diagnosis, and buying a probiotic does not establish the cause or replace appropriate treatment.

What is a healthy vaginal microbiome?

Many people of reproductive age have vaginal communities rich in Lactobacillus species, which produce lactic acid and help maintain an acidic environment. Communities differ between individuals and across life stages; there is no fixed count of 50 species or single bacterial recipe that proves health for everyone. Having fewer lactobacilli in a report is not, by itself, a reason to treat an otherwise well person.

Hormones, menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, menopause, medicines and sexual exposures can influence the local environment. Douching can disturb it. New or multiple partners and not using condoms are associated with BV, but symptoms do not prove poor hygiene or infidelity. Do not stop prescribed contraception because you assume every hormone method causes BV; risks differ by condition and method.

Symptoms overlap: testing matters

Fishy or different odour, altered discharge, itching, burning, soreness and pain with sex or urination may occur with different conditions. BV, candidiasis and trichomoniasis need different treatment; irritants, skin conditions and low-estrogen changes can also cause discomfort. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection, not simply a consequence of lacking “good bacteria.”

Assessment may involve your symptoms, medicines, pregnancy possibility, sexual history, a consensual examination and a vaginal swab, microscopy or a molecular test. Urinary symptoms may need a separate urine assessment. Neither discharge colour, a home pH reading nor a commercial microbiome score diagnoses every cause. Tell the clinician about products already used, and ask about appropriate STI testing.

Bacterial vaginosis, or BV

BV involves a change toward a mixed community of BV-associated bacteria. It may cause thin white or grey discharge and a fishy odour, while many people have no symptoms. Vaginal pH is often above 4.5, but pH alone is not diagnostic; clinicians use combined findings or validated tests. Burning or itching should not automatically be attributed to BV.

Symptomatic BV is usually treated with a prescribed antibiotic, such as metronidazole or clindamycin, by a suitable oral or vaginal regimen. Pregnancy symptoms should be assessed and treated with an appropriate option. Recurrence is common and deserves reassessment rather than endless self-treatment. Ask about other STIs and whether a planned treatment affects condoms; some clindamycin creams weaken latex or rubber barriers.

BV partner advice has changed

Older CDC 2021 guidance does not recommend routine partner treatment based on earlier trials. New evidence led ACOG in October 2025 to advise considering concurrent oral and topical treatment of male partners for adults with recurrent symptomatic BV; shared decisions are advised in some other situations, including same-sex partners and a first symptomatic episode. February 2026 New York State guidance supports offering treatment to ongoing partners of people with symptomatic BV. These are updated approaches with differences in scope, not a universal instruction to treat every past partner.

If BV keeps returning, ask your clinician or sexual-health service about current local partner guidance. The partner needs their own assessment and prescription; do not share medicines or apply vaginal products to a partner without instructions. Discuss avoiding sex until both courses finish, or the appropriate protection if sex occurs, including possible condom weakening by creams. Sharing BV-associated bacteria does not establish exposure to an outside partner.

Yeast infection, or candidiasis

Candida albicans causes many yeast infections, but other species occur. Symptoms can include marked itching, irritation, vulval redness or swelling, soreness, a rash, thick white or sometimes watery discharge, and burning with sex or urine touching inflamed skin. None is specific to yeast. Candida can be present without symptoms and does not always need treatment. Its overgrowth is not explained by a simple rule that lactobacilli are missing.

Antibiotics, pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes, immune suppression and some higher-estrogen exposures can contribute; many uncomplicated cases have no obvious trigger. Treatment may use a suitable local azole cream or vaginal preparation, or oral medicine in selected nonpregnant people. Severe, recurrent or persistent symptoms need testing and a tailored plan, sometimes for another yeast species. During pregnancy CDC recommends a topical azole for 7 days; oral fluconazole should not be used. Ask before self-treating, and return if symptoms persist after an over-the-counter course or recur within two months.

Trichomoniasis is an STI

Trichomonas vaginalis is a parasite transmitted through sexual contact. It may cause itching, burning, redness, soreness, urinary discomfort and changed clear, white, yellow or green discharge with an unusual smell, but it can be symptomless. Testing is needed; neither probiotics nor a yeast treatment cures it. A prescribed oral nitroimidazole is used, commonly metronidazole; vaginal metronidazole gel does not adequately treat trichomoniasis.

Current partners should be evaluated and treated even without symptoms. Avoid sex until you and partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved; discuss other STI tests. CDC recommends retesting sexually active women around three months after treatment because reinfection is common. Symptomatic pregnant patients should be tested and treated at any stage; tinidazole should be avoided during pregnancy. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, allergies and other medicines affect the prescription.

Urinary infection is a separate possibility

A UTI usually starts when bacteria enter the urinary tract through the urethra, often from the bowel. The urethra lies near the vagina, but a UTI is not automatically a vaginal infection or proof of a microbiome imbalance. Burning, urgency, frequent small amounts and lower abdominal discomfort may occur. Cloudy or strong-smelling urine alone does not prove infection; colour changes can have several causes.

A shorter urethra increases susceptibility. Sex, spermicide use, some diaphragm use, menopause, pregnancy, urinary blockage or poor emptying, immune suppression or diabetes, a catheter and recent urinary procedures can matter. Tell the clinician your relevant history rather than blaming cleanliness or partner number. A urine test or culture may help in selected circumstances; treatment depends on pregnancy, health, likely bacteria and local resistance. Some lower UTIs can be managed differently, while kidney or severe infection may need hospital and intravenous antibiotics.

What probiotics can and cannot do

Probiotics are live microorganisms intended to provide a health benefit when given in appropriate amounts. They may be bacteria or yeasts, found in certain foods or supplements. A benefit for one digestive problem or one studied strain does not prove benefit for the vagina. A product labelled Lactobacillus acidophilus is not a demonstrated cure for every infection.

CDC guidance does not support available probiotic products as an established adjunct or replacement treatment for BV, and finds no substantial evidence for treating candidiasis with probiotics. Research into specific preparations continues, but it does not validate every shop product or guarantee restoration after antibiotics. Probiotics do not treat trichomoniasis or an acute UTI. Discuss supplements first, especially with serious illness or immune suppression; do not delay prescribed care.

Gentle care and follow-up

Wash the external vulval skin gently with water or a recommended bland emollient; do not scrub or wash inside the vagina. Avoid douches, perfumed washes, sprays and unprescribed products. Do not insert food or yogurt, essential oils or homemade mixtures. Comfortable clothing and avoiding irritants may help comfort but do not replace treatment of a diagnosed infection.

Complete prescribed courses and follow method-specific instructions. Contact the service if symptoms do not settle or return, rather than repeatedly using leftover antibiotics, antifungals or a “flora reset.” Tell the clinician if pregnant or breastfeeding. Keep a record of symptoms, treatments, test results and recurrences so assessment can distinguish persistent infection, reinfection and noninfectious causes.

When to seek prompt or emergency care

Seek urgent same-day assessment for fever or chills, back or side pain under the ribs, worsening pelvic or lower abdominal pain, vomiting, suspected UTI in pregnancy or with diabetes or immune suppression, or visible or suspected urine blood even once, in a small amount or if uncertain. These may signal kidney infection or another condition. Pregnant patients should discuss new unusual discharge, itching, soreness or painful urination with maternity care promptly; any vaginal bleeding needs immediate maternity advice.

Severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, unusual drowsiness, breathing difficulty or severe illness require emergency care now, especially if pregnancy is possible. Do not wait for a probiotic or a scheduled swab to work. New symptoms after sexual exposure, a first suspected infection or recurrent symptoms also deserve clinical assessment rather than a diagnosis from odour alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Arrange an assessment rather than diagnosing an infection from odour, discharge colour or a home pH result. Tell the clinician about symptoms, pregnancy, medicines and recent sexual exposures so testing and treatment match the cause.

If bacterial vaginosis recurs, ask your clinician or sexual-health service about current local partner-treatment advice. Partners need their own assessment and prescription; do not share medicines.

Do not delay proven care for a probiotic or insert food, oils or homemade remedies. In pregnancy, ask before treatment: topical azoles for seven days are recommended for yeast infection, while oral fluconazole and tinidazole should be avoided.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record symptoms, treatment, tests and questions. It cannot diagnose an infection or microbiome disorder, decide a partner’s prescription, validate a probiotic, or replace STI testing and urgent care.

When to seek help

Do not douche or insert food, oils or homemade remedies. Fever, flank pain, worsening pelvic pain, suspected UTI in pregnancy or with diabetes or immune suppression, or possible urine blood needs urgent same-day assessment. Severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion or breathing difficulty require emergency care now. Do not self-start oral fluconazole in pregnancy or share antibiotics.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The vaginal microbiome varies; one bacterial count or pH result does not define health or diagnose infection.
  • BV, yeast, trichomoniasis and UTIs overlap in symptoms but need different assessment and treatment.
  • Newer BV partner-treatment guidance differs from older CDC advice; ask about your situation and local recommendations.
  • Probiotics do not replace proven treatment or guarantee a restored vaginal microbiome.
  • Pregnancy, fever, flank pain, urine blood or severe illness change how urgently to seek help.

Frequently asked questions

What is a probiotic?

A live microorganism given in an appropriate amount for a health benefit. Benefits are strain- and condition-specific; a gut benefit does not prove that a supplement treats vaginal symptoms.

Is BV the same as any vaginal imbalance?

No. BV is a particular change in vaginal bacterial communities, often with thin discharge or fishy odour, but it can be symptomless. Yeast, an STI and irritation can resemble it; assessment establishes the likely cause.

What can a yeast infection feel like?

Itching, soreness, irritation, redness, a rash, altered white or watery discharge and burning with sex or urination may occur. These are not specific to yeast. Pregnancy, recurrence or failed treatment needs clinical advice.

What symptoms can a UTI cause?

Burning, urgency, frequent small amounts and lower abdominal pain can occur. Cloudiness or smell alone is not proof. Fever, flank pain, pregnancy or suspected urine blood requires urgent same-day advice; confusion or severe illness needs emergency care.

Should my partner be treated for recurrent BV?

Possibly. ACOG 2025 and New York State 2026 guidance support discussing concurrent treatment of ongoing partners in defined situations, while older CDC guidance differs. Ask the clinician; do not share medicines. Recurrent BV does not prove infidelity.

Can probiotics replace an antibiotic or antifungal?

No. Available products are not established substitutes or guaranteed additions for BV or yeast, and do not treat trichomoniasis or an acute UTI. Research on a specific strain cannot be applied to every product.

What changes during pregnancy?

Ask about new symptoms rather than self-treating. Symptomatic BV or trichomoniasis needs appropriate assessment and treatment. Yeast treatment uses a topical azole for 7 days under current CDC advice, not oral fluconazole; tinidazole should be avoided in pregnancy.

Does trichomoniasis need partner care and retesting?

Yes. Current partners need assessment and treatment even without symptoms; avoid sex until treatment is complete for everyone and symptoms have resolved. Sexually active women should be retested around three months; discuss other STI tests.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
